assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reproducible, large room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions was an original experimental discovery, and the later coherent-tunnelling MgO junctions turned it into the read-head and MRAM technology. It is a clear case of a verified experiment with major technological consequence, and it follows naturally from the 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance.
assessment.attribution: The 1995 room-temperature TMR observations from the Miyazaki and Moodera groups are the original experiments, and the high-TMR MgO(001) junctions were realised by Yuasa (and, independently, by Parkin and colleagues, who are not among the credited names). A three-person prize on these names is plausible, but the MgO result has competing claimants and the early history (Julliere 1975) should be checked carefully.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of independent confirmation and industrial deployment; the physics is stable and timing is mature, if anything late.
uncertainties: Parkin's independent MgO work is outside the credited names and could complicate the allocation.
Julliere's 1975 low-temperature precursor is not credited and priority over the earliest observation must be settled.
I rely on my own recollection of the history rather than independently verified records.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new tunable platform for strongly correlated physics, and moire engineering is now a broad field. The experiments are clear, reproducible and observed directly in devices, and the underlying theoretical prediction of a magic angle was specific and quantitative.
assessment.attribution: Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental observations (2018); Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle in 2011. This supports a theory-plus-experiment configuration with three names, though the experimental team (including the lead student) and other twistronics contributors raise allocation questions.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced by many independent groups within a few years; the field is still evolving and the origin of superconductivity remains debated, so some parts of the interpretation are not settled.
uncertainties: The mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Other contributors to moire and twisted-layer physics may be argued to deserve credit.
Long-term practical benefit is not yet demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction and experimental realisation of the quantum spin Hall effect and three-dimensional topological insulators created a new class of quantum matter with robust surface or edge states. The work has had deep influence on condensed-matter physics and materials discovery, and the key claims were confirmed by direct measurement of transport and ARPES.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele predicted the Z2 topological insulator, Molenkamp's group measured the quantum spin Hall edge transport in HgTe (2007), and Hasan's ARPES work demonstrated the three-dimensional phase in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3. The credited list has four names and omits other theorists; I would favour an experiment-weighted trio but Mele's role next to Kane is a real difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many materials, with mature theory; timing is appropriate, though there are concerns about the number of deserving contributors.
uncertainties: Mele is left out of the proposed trio and the Kane-Mele pairing is hard to split.
Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and others (not in the credited list) contributed the HgTe proposal.
The practical benefit is mainly future-oriented.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Solid-state femtosecond lasers, from Ti:sapphire gain media to Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable-absorber mode locking, are enabling instruments for ultrafast science and metrology and underpin attosecond physics, which the committee recognised in 2023. This is an invention-type prize built on new tools that open doors to phenomena not previously accessible.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed the Ti:sapphire laser, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode locking, and Keller invented the SESAM for self-starting, robust passive mode locking. The division among three distinct inventions is sensible but the Kerr-lens priority (including work outside the supplied list) is a source of uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: Decades of universal use and independent confirmation; recognition has arguably been long awaited and the technology is mature.
uncertainties: Priority for Kerr-lens mode locking involves people beyond the credited names.
Overlap with the 2018 chirped-pulse and 2023 attosecond prizes may weaken novelty in the committee's eyes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers provide femtosecond coherent X-ray pulses and have opened time-resolved structural and electronic studies of matter at atomic resolution. As an invention verified in working facilities, it is a transformative tool with wide impact in physics, chemistry and biology.
assessment.attribution: The self-amplified spontaneous emission concept and its theory trace to Pellegrini and collaborators and Kim, while Rossbach led the first soft X-ray SASE facility development; the credit is spread over many accelerator and laser physicists and the supplied trio may exclude important contributors such as those who demonstrated lasing at LCLS.
assessment.maturity: Operating for over a decade at several facilities with independent confirmation; the technique is mature although scientific payoff is still accumulating.
uncertainties: Accelerator physics collaborations make individual attribution difficult.
Madey's original free-electron laser and the LCLS experimental team are not in the credited names.
It may be viewed as accelerator engineering rather than a physics discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single spins in diamond and related colour centres are a versatile solid-state quantum platform for sensing at the nanoscale and for quantum networks. It is an experimentally verified, instrument-oriented advance that I find attractive for its measurement applications.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated single-NV optical detection of spin in 1997, Awschalom's group pioneered coherent spin control in several defect systems, and Lukin contributed key sensing and network demonstrations. Walsworth and many others made major sensing contributions, so a three-person limit forces difficult choices.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations and growing applications, but the field is still expanding and the decisive application is not yet fixed.
uncertainties: Four credited names with a three-laureate limit and large wider community.
Recognition may be premature relative to future quantum-technology outcomes.
Priority among sensing and quantum-register milestones is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics demonstrated strong coupling between superconducting qubits and microwave photons and became the dominant architecture for superconducting quantum processors. The experimental demonstration and the theoretical proposal were both clear and important.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf proposed the architecture and Wallraff et al. (2004) provided the first strong-coupling experiment; the supplied trio is plausible but Girvin and other Yale contributors are absent from the list.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and widely adopted, though the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits reduces the immediate room for another superconducting-circuit award.
uncertainties: Recent prize in neighbouring area may argue for waiting.
Girvin and other contributors are not credited.
Attribution between proposal and first experiment is delicate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus sensor and the functionalised-tip non-contact atomic force microscopy that resolves the bond structure of individual molecules are real advances in instrumentation, letting people see matter at a scale that was previously inaccessible. I weigh this seriously from my microscopy background.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus tuning-fork sensor, while Gross, Meyer and colleagues demonstrated CO-tip imaging of molecular structure (2009). A fair trio exists but the dependence on earlier scanning-probe prizes (1986) and the contributions of others to frequency-modulation AFM complicate originality.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced and widely used, but it is a refinement of an already honoured technique and its broader impact is more specialised.
uncertainties: Novelty relative to the 1986 scanning-probe prize may be judged insufficient.
The broader impact beyond surface science is uncertain.
I cannot independently verify detailed priority claims.
